assignments.html:
VR ACTIVITY
Follow the Container
Solo · one in-headset session
16 points · file upload or text entry
◉ ◌ ◉
Before you start

Finish both lessons and read both sources first. Your notes from each page are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the page, so open it before you write. Then write your answers and submit them in this assignment.

WHAT YOU'RE DOING

In 1956 a single ship carried fifty-eight truck bodies packed in its hold, and the shipping container changed how the world trades. In your VR headset you will follow a container through a reconstruction of a modern port and the chain that carries goods from a factory to a shop. Your task is to find evidence of who gains and who is strained along the way.

WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset, charged and ready
▶
Your course page for this week, which lists the session link and the place to enter
▶
A notebook or open document for quick notes while you are in the session
▶
About 45 minutes in one sitting
HOW TO JOIN
Where to go: Open your immersive session from the link on your course page, then enter the location named there.
Solo or group: Solo. You do not need a partner.
If something fails: Write down what happened and use the help contact on your course page. Do not skip the activity.
WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Review first. Reread the sections of the lesson “A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science” called Trade Without Walls and Uniting or Dividing. Remember that cheaper shipping let goods be made far from where they are sold, and that the gains and costs fell on different people.
2
Start at the factory end. Begin where the goods are made or loaded, and note how the work is organized and how many people it needs.
3
Follow the box. Move with a container from the ship to the crane, the train, and the truck. Notice how little a person has to open or touch it along the way.
4
Stop at three places. Choose three spots that show a gain or a cost of this system. At each one, capture a picture with your headset and jot a note about what you see.
5
Look for the people. At each spot, ask who has a job because of this system, who might have lost one, and who is not on the chain at all.
6
Write your response. After you leave the session, write one paragraph of about 150 to 200 words that answers this question: Who gains and who is strained along this chain, and what can a model of a port never tell you about the people whose lives depend on it?
WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit your three captured images and your paragraph in the Canvas assignment. Use the images as evidence in your writing, and name which picture you are referring to.

Estimated time: 45 minutes

SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I followed a container from the ship to the end of the chain.
☐
I captured three images that show different parts of the port or chain.
☐
My paragraph uses at least two of my images as evidence.
☐
My paragraph connects what I saw to what I read about trade and globalization in the lesson “A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science”.
☐
I wrote in complete sentences and kept to about 150 to 200 words.
FACILITATOR NOTE

Teacher-facing. Before releasing this activity, add the session link and the specific location to the course page, and confirm that students have a way to capture images in their headsets. The instructions above assume a walkable reconstruction of a container port and its supply chain. If none is available, substitute another walkable space that shows how goods move around the world, such as a model of a factory and a shipping route, and adjust the steps and review section to match, and note the substitution in the teacher's manual. The instructions are platform-neutral on purpose. Grade with the course rubric for VR activities: three images as evidence, a paragraph that cites them, and reasoning tied to the lesson.

MODULE INTRO
The Modern World
2 questions · survey · one attempt
◉ ◌ ◉
Essential question for this week
How did religion, revolution, terror, trade, and technology reshape the world after 1945?
Instructions

Welcome to The Modern World. This short check-in is not graded. Your answers help your teacher see where each student is starting, so answer honestly.

What you will be able to do

Religion, Revolution, and Terror: Iran 1979 to 9/11

  • Explain how the Iranian Revolution of 1979 replaced a monarchy with a government led by religious authorities.
  • Describe how the war in Afghanistan helped give rise to al-Qaeda and the Taliban.
  • Describe the attacks of September 11, 2001, and the choices that led to them.

A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science

  • Describe how trade, technology, and political change tied the world's economies more closely together after 1945.
  • Explain how European integration began with the Schuman Declaration and grew into the European Union.
  • Evaluate the gains and strains that globalization brought to different peoples.

quizzes.title: Quarterly Exam: Quarter 4: Late Modernity
quizzes.description:
QUARTERLY EXAM
The Modern World
42 questions · 41 points · one attempt
◉ ◌ ◉
About this exam

This exam covers this quarter only. It has 41 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

Before you start

Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you start. Then choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: Why did industrialization begin in Britain and not somewhere else?

answers.text: Britain had more people than any other country, so it had more workers for its mills.
The Crown ordered the building of the first factories and paid for each of them.
Cheap coal and fairly high wages made machines that saved labor a good bargain.
Britain had banned the export of cotton, so its mills had no foreign rivals.

questions.feedback_correct: Coal lay close to the surface and the sea. Settled government, canals, savings, and skilled craftsmen did the rest. Nobody planned it, and none of it made the outcome certain.

questions.text: How did Watt's improved steam engine change where factories could be built?

answers.text: It could turn a wheel, so a factory no longer had to sit beside a fast river.
It could run on wood alone, so factories could be built far from the coal mines.
It was small enough to be built into each worker's cottage.
It made the water wheel faster, so more factories were built on rivers.

questions.feedback_correct: Watt's separate condenser used far less coal. After Watt and Boulton became partners in 1775, a factory could stand anywhere a cart of coal could reach.

questions.text: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do that earlier appeals had not?

answers.text: It banned all work by women and children in every kind of factory.
It set a ten-hour day for every worker in every trade.
It gave the workers the right to vote in the next election.
It created paid inspectors to see that the law was kept.

questions.feedback_correct: It barred children under nine from textile mills and limited the hours of older children. The Ten Hours Act of 1847 came later.

questions.text: Marx expected the workers of the most industrial country to rebel first. What happened in Britain?

answers.text: The workers rose in 1848 and the army put down the revolt in a few days.
Wages rose, unions grew, and Parliament widened the vote for workers.
The mill owners gave their factories to the workers and left the country.
Parliament banned all unions and the workers were too afraid to protest.

questions.feedback_correct: The revolutions that later took Marx's name broke out in Russia, a farming country.

questions.text: What did the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 do?

answers.text: They gave each German state a written constitution and an elected assembly.
They put universities under watch, banned student clubs, and censored books.
They joined Austria and Prussia into a single country under one emperor.
They freed the peasants of Prussia from the dues that they owed to the nobles.

questions.feedback_correct: Metternich used the murder of Kotzebue to push them through the German Confederation. Spies and police were common.

questions.text: Why did the Frankfurt assembly of 1848 fail to unite Germany?

answers.text: The Austrian army occupied Frankfurt on the first day of the meeting.
The assembly voted to unite with France and the Germans refused to follow.
The assembly could not agree on a language for the new constitution.
The Prussian king refused its crown, and the assembly had no army to back it.

questions.feedback_correct: Frederick William IV would not take a crown from an assembly of commoners or break with the German princes. The assembly was scattered in 1849.

questions.text: How did Garibaldi help to unite Italy?

answers.text: He took the south with a force of volunteers and handed it to the king.
He defeated the Austrians at Solferino and took Venetia for Piedmont.
He persuaded the pope to give up Rome and join the new kingdom.
He led the army of Piedmont in the war of 1859 and signed the peace.

questions.feedback_correct: In May 1860 he landed in Sicily with volunteers in red shirts. He then met Victor Emmanuel II, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861.

questions.text: How did Bismarck use the telegram from Ems in 1870?

answers.text: He kept it secret so that France would be taken by surprise.
He sent it to the Austrians to persuade them to join Prussia.
He edited it to sound sharper, and the French government declared war.
He published it unchanged to prove that the French had insulted the king.

questions.feedback_correct: The southern German states then joined Prussia. William was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871.

questions.text: Which developments helped Europeans conquer so much of Africa after 1870?

answers.text: Railways that crossed the whole of Africa before 1850 and cheap iron ships.
Alliances with every African ruler and the consent of the Berlin conference.
Large European armies that landed in Africa and stayed for several years.
Steamships, the telegraph, quinine, and the Maxim gun gave Europeans an edge.

questions.feedback_correct: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and shortened voyages. Quinine protected Europeans against malaria, and breech-loading rifles gave small forces great firepower.

questions.text: Why did Ethiopia keep its independence when most of Africa did not?

answers.text: Britain and France agreed at Berlin that Ethiopia should be left alone.
Menelik II bought modern rifles, trained his army, and won at Adwa.
Ethiopia had no valuable land, and the Europeans were not interested.
The emperor signed a treaty that made Ethiopia a protectorate of Italy.

questions.feedback_correct: Ethiopia and Liberia were the only African lands to keep their independence.

questions.text: What event in 1839 turned the dispute over the opium trade into the First Opium War?

answers.text: The Qianlong Emperor refused Macartney's request for freer trade in 1793.
The Taiping rebels attacked the British ships at Shanghai.
Lin Zexu destroyed British opium, and merchants demanded payment.
Britain wanted to stop the sale of opium in China, and China refused.

questions.feedback_correct: Lin seized and destroyed more than twenty thousand chests in 1839. Some in Parliament thought the war a disgrace, but a fleet was sent.

questions.text: What did the samurai of Satsuma and Choshu learn from the Western bombardments of 1863 and 1864?

answers.text: Swords could not expel foreigners; they had to learn Western ways.
The shogun was strong enough to defeat the Western ships without their help.
Japan should sign treaties with every nation and give up its own army.
The emperor should give up his throne and move to the city of Edo.

questions.feedback_correct: In January 1868 these samurai seized the palace in Kyoto and declared the emperor restored to power.

questions.text: How did the Schlieffen Plan make war more likely in 1914?

answers.text: It called for a quick blow at France before the slower Russians could mobilize.
It required Germany to wait for an attack by France before it could mobilize.
It promised Britain that Germany would respect the neutrality of Belgium.
It asked Austria to attack Russia first and then take the Balkans.

questions.feedback_correct: All the plans depended on speed, and each country's mobilization looked like an act of war to its neighbors.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call the death of Franz Ferdinand ironic?

answers.text: He was killed by an assassin sent by his own government.
He had ordered the driver to turn right on that street.
He had often argued against going to war with Serbia, fearing for his empire.
He had planned to give Bosnia to Serbia within a year.

questions.feedback_correct: Princip stepped forward because the driver took a wrong turn and stopped to back up in front of a delicatessen.

questions.text: Why did attacks on the Western Front so often fail?

answers.text: Both armies lacked shells, and they could not keep up their bombardments.
Machine guns and artillery gave the men defending a trench line a decisive advantage.
The armies were too small to man a line that ran from the Channel to Switzerland.
The generals ordered every attack to begin in daylight, and soldiers refused.

questions.feedback_correct: On the first day of the Somme, nearly sixty thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. By November the line had moved only a few miles.

questions.text: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917. What did this help to bring about?

answers.text: The end of the British blockade of Germany and the return of food.
The surrender of Russia and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
The collapse of Austria-Hungary and the end of the Habsburg throne.
The entry of the United States into the war on the Allied side.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress declared war on April 6, 1917. Soon more than a million American soldiers were in France.

questions.text: Why did Clemenceau want a harsh peace?

answers.text: He believed Germany had been punished enough and wanted to move on quickly.
He wanted Germany to join the League of Nations as soon as possible.
France had lost over a million men and was invaded twice in fifty years.
He had promised Wilson that France would take no land from Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: Wilson had hoped for self-determination and a League. Lloyd George feared pushing Germany too hard.

questions.text: How did the Bolsheviks win the civil war against the Whites?

answers.text: Britain, France, Japan, and the United States sent large armies to help the Reds.
The Reds had many more soldiers than the Whites in every battle.
The Whites were driven out when Lenin gave land to the nobles.
The Whites were divided, and the Reds held the cities and railways.

questions.feedback_correct: The war lasted until 1921 and famine and fighting killed millions. Foreign troops came at various times, but not enough to matter.

questions.text: What caused the German hyperinflation of 1923?

answers.text: France occupied the Ruhr, and the government printed money to pay striking workers.
The Dawes Plan ended all American loans to Germany in 1923.
The stock market in New York crashed and the banks in Germany failed.
The Kaiser returned and ordered the treasury to pay his old soldiers.

questions.feedback_correct: The government printed money to pay striking workers, and the savings of the middle class vanished.

questions.text: What did Stalin, Mussolini, and Hitler have in common, despite their differences?

answers.text: Each came to power by winning more than half of the votes in free elections.
One party, one leader, a secret police, and an enemy within.
Each was supported by the Church and by the old nobility.
Each ruled through an elected parliament that had real power over taxes.

questions.feedback_correct: They took advantage of fear, humiliation, and economic ruin. In each case particular decisions by other people also mattered.

questions.text: What did the Munich agreement of 1938 cost Czechoslovakia?

answers.text: Its alliance with France, which was ended at once by the French parliament.
Its mountain defenses, and in 1939 the rest of the country.
Its army, which was disbanded by order of the four powers.
Its government, which was moved to London during the war.

questions.feedback_correct: This broke Hitler's promise and showed that his aims went beyond Germans living outside Germany.

questions.text: How were the Germans able to defeat France in about six weeks in 1940?

answers.text: Tanks crossed the Ardennes, a forest that the French thought impassable for armor.
They broke through the Maginot Line with heavy artillery in a single week.
They had many more tanks and planes than France and Britain combined.
They landed from the sea in Normandy and took Paris by surprise.

questions.feedback_correct: The tanks reached the Channel in ten days and trapped the British and some French forces at Dunkirk.

questions.text: How did Nazi persecution of the Jews move through stages?

answers.text: From a boycott of shops to a ban on travel, and then expulsion of all Jews to Palestine.
From a ban on marriage to a boycott, and then to a peace treaty at Wannsee.
From removing rights to violence, ghettos, shootings, and killing centers.
From laws to violence, and then to a vote by the Reichstag to end the war.

questions.feedback_correct: The Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, the ghettos, the Einsatzgruppen, and the killing centers were successive steps. The Final Solution was coordinated at Wannsee in January 1942.

questions.text: A crime of this size needed many hands. What does the lesson say about the people who took part?

answers.text: Nearly all of them were party members who had been ordered to take part.
Nearly all refused to obey, and the plan was carried out by a few.
Nearly all were foreigners brought in from the occupied lands.
Many were not fanatics, though some resisted and rescuers were rare.

questions.feedback_correct: Clerks, police, soldiers, doctors, and engineers played a part. Some, such as the villagers of Le Chambon and the Danes, resisted.

questions.text: What did the Truman Doctrine mark?

answers.text: The end of the Marshall Plan and the withdrawal of American troops from Germany.
A pledge that the United States would never use atomic weapons first.
An alliance of Britain, France, and the Soviet Union to defend Greece.
The United States took on lasting peacetime commitments in Europe.

questions.feedback_correct: Britain could no longer support Greece and Turkey in 1947. Truman asked Congress for aid to free peoples resisting pressure.

questions.text: Why did the Cold War turn into open fighting in Korea but not in Europe?

answers.text: The United Nations took command of the armies of Europe in 1949, but not of Asia's.
In Europe neither side could attack without being destroyed in return.
Both sides gave up their atomic bombs after the Berlin Airlift, but Asia did not.
Korea had atomic weapons of its own, and no nation in Europe had any.

questions.feedback_correct: This was deterrence, sometimes called mutual assured destruction. Fear of nuclear war kept the peace in Europe, yet the contest still spread to other parts of the world, as in Korea in 1950.

questions.text: How did events in Poland help to crack the Soviet bloc?

answers.text: The Polish army overthrew the government and left the Warsaw Pact in 1980.
The Soviet Union gave Poland its freedom in return for coal and grain.
The pope's visit and Solidarity showed millions of Poles they were not alone.
The Polish government welcomed Solidarity and made it the ruling party.

questions.feedback_correct: Martial law in 1981 jailed Solidarity's leaders, but could not kill the movement. In 1989 Solidarity won nearly every seat it was allowed to contest.

questions.text: What did Deng Xiaoping change in China, and what did he keep?

answers.text: He ended the party's rule and held free elections in 1989.
He let farmers and entrepreneurs work for profit, but the party kept power.
He closed the schools and sent the young to the countryside.
He ended the economy of the commune and restored the landlords.

questions.feedback_correct: China's economy began to grow quickly. In June 1989 the party crushed the protests in Tiananmen Square.

questions.text: Why did Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance work against Britain?

answers.text: It depended on an opponent who could be shamed by seeing suffering.
It relied on the British army being too small to arrest the protesters.
It was backed by the Muslim League and by the armies of the princes.
It brought immediate help from the United Nations and the Soviet Union.

questions.feedback_correct: The British had a free press and a conscience. Historians note that the same tactics would have met a different fate against a regime like Stalin's or Hitler's.

questions.text: Which choice by Britain made the partition of India in 1947 harder to manage?

answers.text: It stayed in India until 1950, so the new states had no say in where the border ran.
It ordered the Indian army and the police to stay away from the new border while mobs formed.
It told the princes to stay independent, and several of them went to war over the border.
It set an early date and gave a lawyer who had never seen India a few weeks to draw the lines.

questions.feedback_correct: Mountbatten set the date earlier than expected, and Radcliffe's lines were not published until two days after independence. Perhaps ten to fifteen million people crossed the new lines, and mobs on all sides killed their neighbors.

questions.text: Why did Britain's wartime promises about the Middle East cause so much trouble later?

answers.text: It promised Palestine to the Ottomans and then took it by force.
It made promises to Arabs, to France, and to Zionist leaders.
It promised Egypt independence and then closed the Suez Canal.
It promised all its lands to the League of Nations after the war.

questions.feedback_correct: Hussein of Mecca, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, and the Balfour Declaration could not all be kept.

questions.text: The lesson says that each side tells the story of 1948 differently. How?

answers.text: Palestinians call it a victory, and Israelis call it a defeat.
Both sides call it a civil war, and neither side blames the other.
Palestinians call it the Nakba, and Israelis call it independence.
Israelis call it the Nakba, and Palestinians call it a War of Independence.

questions.feedback_correct: About seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs left or were driven from their homes, and historians continue to debate how many of each.

questions.text: How did the Shah lose his throne in 1979?

answers.text: The army overthrew him and gave power to Khomeini in a single night.
The United States removed him in a plan to put Mossadegh back in power.
Strikes and protests grew after soldiers fired, and the Shah left Iran.
The Iraqi army invaded Iran and the Shah was killed in the fighting.

questions.feedback_correct: The Shah was secretly ill with cancer, and some of his generals lost heart. A different response in 1978 might have kept him on the throne.

questions.text: How did the war in Afghanistan help to give rise to al-Qaeda?

answers.text: The Soviets trained bin Laden, who later turned against them.
Volunteers joined the fight, and bin Laden helped to fund them.
The Taliban built al-Qaeda to defend Afghanistan against the United States.
The United States asked bin Laden to attack its own embassies in Africa.

questions.feedback_correct: After the Soviets left in 1989 the world lost interest, and the Taliban later gave bin Laden a base.

questions.text: What did Robert Schuman propose in 1950?

answers.text: To form a single European army under French and German command.
To make Germany pay reparations in coal and steel to France.
To end all tariffs between the nations of Europe at once.
To put French and German coal and steel under one authority.

questions.feedback_correct: Coal and steel were the stuff of weapons, so such a pact would make war between the two materially impossible. Six nations formed the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951.

questions.text: What does the lesson conclude about the internet and other tools of globalization?

answers.text: They carry both effects, because people, and not tools, decide how they are used.
They are good for the world, and any harm comes from governments that misuse them.
They are harmful to the world, and every nation should limit their use.
They are neutral and have little effect on how people live and think.

questions.feedback_correct: The same network lets a student read the same books as one in a great city, and lets a hidden network spread a lie as quickly as a doctor can share a cure.

questions.text:
Religion played a part too. Many of the early ironmasters, bankers, and manufacturers were Dissenters, Protestants outside the Church of England, such as the Quaker family of Abraham Darby. The law kept Dissenters out of the universities and out of public office. Shut out of those careers, they put their energy into trade, schooling, and invention, and they trusted one another with money because

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: the Church of England stood behind their loans.
answers.feedback: The passage says Dissenters stood outside the Church of England, so it would not have backed their loans.

answers.text: the law required Dissenters to lend to one another.
answers.feedback: No law is said to require this. The passage mentions the law only as keeping Dissenters out of the universities and public office.

answers.text: they already knew one another from the meeting house.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage places the Dissenters' trust in the people they knew from the meeting house.

answers.text: they had studied together at the universities.
answers.feedback: The passage says the law kept Dissenters out of the universities, so they could not have studied there together.

questions.text:
The man who finally succeeded was a practical statesman. Count Camillo di Cavour became prime minister of Piedmont in 1852. He was not a soldier or a romantic. He was a landowner who had experimented with fertilizers and irrigation, and as a minister he built railways, cut tariffs, and strengthened the army. He knew that Piedmont alone could not defeat Austria, so he looked for an ally. He sent about fifteen thousand troops to join Britain and France in the Crimean War, which won him a place at the peace table, where he raised the Italian question before the great powers. In 1858 he met Napoleon III of France in secret and made an agreement: in return for Nice and Savoy, France would help to drive Austria from northern Italy.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Cavour used practical statecraft, building up Piedmont and finding a foreign ally, to prepare the drive against Austria.
answers.feedback: Correct. It covers the whole passage: practical preparation at home and a bargain abroad.

answers.text: Cavour, an idealist who disliked practical politics, gave up Nice and Savoy only to please the French emperor Napoleon III.
answers.feedback: The passage says Cavour was not a romantic, and he traded Nice and Savoy to gain French help, not to please an emperor.

answers.text: Cavour showed that Piedmont could defeat Austria by itself once its railways, tariffs, and army were improved.
answers.feedback: The passage says he knew Piedmont alone could not defeat Austria, which is why he looked for an ally.

answers.text: Cavour's chief achievement was taking part in the Crimean War, which won the support of Britain and France against Austria.
answers.feedback: This is too narrow and misstates the result. The Crimean War won him a place at the peace table, and the ally against Austria was France, by the secret agreement of 1858.

questions.text:
Under collectivization, the state seized their farms and herds and combined them into large collective farms. The wealthier peasants, called kulaks, were labeled enemies, and many were shot or deported to camps. Peasants killed their animals instead of surrendering them. Between 1932 and 1933 a terrible famine struck Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and southern Russia, and millions starved while the state continued to take grain.

Which choice correctly describes how many peasants responded to collectivization and what the state did during the famine of 1932 to 1933?

answers.text: Peasants gave their animals to the state willingly, and the state sent grain to the regions where people starved.
answers.feedback: The passage says peasants killed their animals instead of surrendering them, and that the state kept taking grain.

answers.text: Peasants fled to the cities in large numbers, and the state ended collectivization while the famine lasted.
answers.feedback: The passage does not say peasants fled, and the state continued its policy, taking grain while millions starved.

answers.text: Peasants rose in a general revolt, and the state ordered the kulaks to take over the collective farms.
answers.feedback: The passage mentions no general revolt, and it says the kulaks were labeled enemies, not given the farms.

answers.text: Peasants killed their animals rather than surrender them, and the state kept taking grain during the famine.
answers.feedback: Correct. Both parts match the passage.

questions.text:
By the late 1970s the Soviet economy was stagnating. In 1979 the Soviets invaded Afghanistan, expecting a short campaign, and became trapped in a costly war against local fighters supplied by the West and others.

Which choice would best support the text's claim that the Soviets became trapped in a costly war in Afghanistan?

answers.text: In December 1979 Soviet troops entered Afghanistan in order to prop up a communist government there.
answers.feedback: This explains why the Soviets entered Afghanistan. It shows nothing about the war's cost or about being trapped.

answers.text: The rebels received weapons and money from the United States, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan during the 1980s war.
answers.feedback: Outside supplies help explain how the rebels could fight on, but they do not show what the war cost the Soviets.

answers.text: About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died, and rebels with American Stinger missiles shot down Soviet helicopters.
answers.feedback: Correct. Soldiers killed and helicopters lost are direct evidence of a costly war.

answers.text: Many Afghans, a deeply religious and tribal people, rose up against the communist government in their country.
answers.feedback: This explains why Afghans resisted. It does not show the cost to the Soviets.

questions.text:
The spark came in January 1978, when a newspaper printed an article insulting Khomeini. Students and clerics protested in the holy city of Qom, and police killed some of them. Shia custom marks a death with mourning forty days later, and so each memorial became a new protest, with new deaths and another forty days to come. By September the pattern had spread across the country. On September 8 soldiers fired on a crowd in Tehran's Jaleh Square, and Iranians called the day Black Friday. After that, many who had hoped for a compromise with the Shah gave up on him.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Killings of protesters fed a cycle of mourning and new protests, until many gave up hope of compromise with the Shah.
answers.feedback: Correct. It joins the whole sequence: killings, mourning, spreading protest, and lost hope of compromise.

answers.text: A newspaper article insulting Khomeini was the only cause of the unrest, which spread from the city of Qom to every part of Iran.
answers.feedback: The article was only the spark. The passage is about the protests and deaths that followed, and it names no single cause.

answers.text: Black Friday was the first protest in Iran, and it forced the Shah to leave the country within a few days of it.
answers.feedback: The protests began in January, months before Black Friday, and the passage does not say the Shah left then.

answers.text: Shia custom forbade public protest, so the crowds stayed quiet until soldiers fired on them in Tehran in September.
answers.feedback: The passage says each memorial became a new protest, so custom fed the protests instead of forbidding them.

questions.text: In a few sentences, describe the test-taking strategy you used on this exam. What did you do first, and how did you decide between answer choices?

quizzes.title: Quarter 4 Exam (SAT)
quizzes.description:
QUARTERLY EXAM, SAT-STYLE
The Modern World
49 questions · 46 points · one attempt
◉ ◌ ◉
About this exam

This exam covers this quarter only. It has 36 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. Every question gives you a short passage taken from your lessons, so you can answer from the passage itself. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

Before you start

Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you start. Then choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text:
Coal mines had a constant problem: water seeped in and flooded the shafts. In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built an engine that used steam to pump water out. It swallowed huge amounts of coal, but that hardly mattered at a coal mine, where fuel was nearly free. Anywhere else, coal had to be hauled in by cart, and the engine cost too much to run. So it stayed at the mines, and for half a century nobody did much better.

According to the text, why did Newcomen's engine stay at the mines?

answers.text: It was too heavy to move by cart, and no engineer had yet learned to make it smaller.
answers.feedback: The text gives the cost of running it, not its weight, as the reason.

answers.text: Parliament had given the mine owners a patent that kept the engine out of other businesses.
answers.feedback: The text mentions no such patent. It says the engine was too costly to run away from the mines.

answers.text: Coal was nearly free at the mines, while anywhere else the engine cost too much to run.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: It could pump water only from deep shafts, so it was of no use in a factory or a mill.
answers.feedback: The text says the reason was the cost of coal, not what the engine could do.

questions.text:
Think about what that combination meant for a business owner. When workers are costly and fuel is cheap, a machine that saves labor and burns coal is a good bargain.

Which choice best supports the idea that machines that saved labor paid off in Britain?

answers.text: Hargreaves's spinning jenny let one worker spin many threads at once instead of one.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Newcomen, an ironmonger, built an engine that used steam to pump water out of coal mines.
answers.feedback: This describes who built the pump, not how labor-saving machines paid off.

answers.text: The Darby family were Quakers, Dissenters who were shut out of the universities and public office.
answers.feedback: This is a fact about religion and has nothing to do with labor-saving machines.

answers.text: After 1688 Parliament and the courts protected property, so an investor could keep what he earned.
answers.feedback: This explains why investors felt safe, not why machines that saved labor paid off.

questions.text:
Smith was no flatterer of employers when it came to wages, either. He wrote that masters were always and everywhere in a sort of quiet but steady agreement not to raise wages above their usual rate, and that when workers combined, the law came down on them far harder than it did on masters who did the same. A reader in the 1820s could set that remark beside the Combination Acts and draw a conclusion Smith himself might have shared.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: A reader in the 1820s could set Smith's remark beside the Combination Acts and draw a conclusion.
answers.feedback: This is only one sentence in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Economists in Smith's day all agreed that employers should have no say in setting wages for their workers.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and the passage does not say what other economists thought.

answers.text: Smith argued that workers should be forbidden to combine, since masters never did the same thing.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says the law was harder on workers than on masters who combined.

answers.text: Smith saw that employers quietly agreed to hold wages down, and the law fell harder on workers who combined.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
The same Parliament that passed the Factory Act reformed poor relief in 1834. Under the new Poor Law, an able-bodied man who asked for help had to enter a workhouse, where families were separated and the food was meant to be plainer than what a laborer could earn outside. The aim was to push men toward work and to cut the cost of relief. Many of the poor came to ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: prefer the workhouse to work in the mills and mines.
answers.feedback: The passage says the workhouse was made harsh on purpose, so few would prefer it.

answers.text: dread the workhouse and avoid asking for any kind of help.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: welcome the new law as a generous reform of relief.
answers.feedback: The passage says the law was meant to push men toward work and cut the cost of relief.

answers.text: ignore the new law, since few were ever sent to workhouses.
answers.feedback: The passage says an able-bodied man who asked for help had to enter one.

questions.text:
The Congress nearly broke up over two prizes. Alexander wanted Poland, and Prussia wanted the German kingdom of Saxony, whose king had stayed loyal to Napoleon too long. Britain and Austria feared a Russia and a Prussia grown so large. Talleyrand saw his opening. He argued that the settlement should rest on legitimacy, and that the king of Saxony, whatever his faults, had a right to his throne. In January 1815 France joined Britain and Austria in a secret treaty to stand against Russia and Prussia if it came to that. War was close. The quarrel ended in a compromise. Russia received most of Poland, and Prussia received only part of Saxony, along with its lands on the Rhine.

According to the text, how was the quarrel over Poland and Saxony settled?

answers.text: Prussia received all of Saxony, and Russia received only part of Poland.
answers.feedback: This reverses the outcome the text gives.

answers.text: Russia received most of Poland, and Prussia received only part of Saxony.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: Poland became an independent kingdom, and Saxony stayed whole under its own king.
answers.feedback: The text says Russia received most of Poland and Prussia received part of Saxony.

answers.text: Britain and Austria gave up both lands to avoid a war with Russia and Prussia.
answers.feedback: The text says Britain and Austria feared a larger Russia and Prussia and stood against them.

questions.text:
The diplomats showed prudence, which is the habit of weighing consequences before acting, and moderation toward the defeated. A harsher peace might have made France a permanent enemy.

Which choice best supports the claim that the diplomats were moderate toward France?

answers.text: In 1814 the diplomats joined Belgium to the Netherlands to guard against a French attack.
answers.feedback: This shows how the powers protected themselves from France, not moderation toward it.

answers.text: Talleyrand argued that the settlement should rest on legitimacy, since the king of Saxony had a right to his throne.
answers.feedback: This describes a point about Saxony, not how the powers treated France.

answers.text: Prince Metternich hosted the Congress, while its real work went on in small committees and private talks.
answers.feedback: This describes how the Congress worked, not how it treated France.

answers.text: In 1818 the powers withdrew their armies of occupation from France and admitted it to their councils.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

questions.text:
Was it the leaders, or was it deeper forces? In both countries, the answer is a mixture. Nationalism, railways, and trade made unity attractive and likely. But the actual shape of the new states depended on particular decisions: Napoleon III's secret bargain, Garibaldi's gamble, King William's choice of Bismarck, and Bismarck's restraint after Königgrätz. A Germany that included Austria was entirely possible. So was an Italy of two or three kingdoms. If Frederick William IV had accepted the crown at Frankfurt in 1849, a very different Germany might have been born.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Unity came from deep forces such as nationalism and railways, shaped by the choices of a few men.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Frederick William IV's refusal of the crown at Frankfurt in 1849 changed the shape of Germany.
answers.feedback: This is one example in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Great nations are always made by strong leaders and never by the slow pressure of deeper forces.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and it contradicts the passage, which gives both causes a place.

answers.text: Nationalism alone made unity certain, so the decisions of individual leaders made little difference.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says the shape of the new states depended on particular decisions.

questions.text:
Here Bismarck showed his judgment. The king and the generals wanted to march on Vienna and take land. Bismarck argued against it, so fiercely that he was close to resigning, until the Crown Prince helped to bring the old king around. He took no Austrian territory, because he wanted ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: to leave land free for a later war against Austria.
answers.feedback: This reverses his reasoning. He argued against taking land so that Austria would not become an enemy.

answers.text: to please the generals who wanted a quick peace.
answers.feedback: The passage says the king and the generals wanted to take land, and Bismarck argued against them.

answers.text: Austria as a friend in the years that were to follow.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: to avoid angering the Russian tsar who stood behind Austria.
answers.feedback: Nothing in the passage connects the tsar to this decision.

questions.text:
Before the canal, a ship from London to Bombay had to sail around the Cape of Good Hope, a voyage of more than ten thousand miles. Through the canal the trip was about forty percent shorter. Steamers also needed coaling stations along the way, because a ship cannot burn what it does not carry, and so ports such as Malta, Aden, and Port Said became valuable for their own sake. A great power that wanted to move quickly needed friendly harbors every few days of steaming, and that fact pulled governments into places they had never cared about before.

According to the text, why did ports such as Malta, Aden, and Port Said become valuable?

answers.text: They lay beside the Cape of Good Hope, which every ship from London to Bombay still had to round.
answers.feedback: The text says the canal let ships avoid the Cape.

answers.text: They were the only ports where quinine could be bought to protect crews from malaria and fever.
answers.feedback: The text mentions quinine in another place and does not connect it to these ports.

answers.text: They were the homes of the licensed merchants who traded with every steamer that passed through.
answers.feedback: The text gives coaling stations as the reason, not licensed merchants.

answers.text: Steamers needed coaling stations, and ships needed friendly harbors every few days of steaming.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

questions.text:
Reports by missionaries and a British shipping clerk, Edmund Morel, produced a public outcry. Morel noticed that ships from the Congo reached Antwerp loaded with rubber, while the ships going out carried soldiers and guns instead of trade goods, and he saw what that meant. A British consul, Roger Casement, confirmed the abuses in a report in 1904. In 1908 the Belgian government took the Congo from the king.

Which choice best supports the claim that public opinion at home pushed Belgium to end Leopold's rule?

answers.text: Stanley's agents made hundreds of treaties with local chiefs in exchange for cloth and trinkets.
answers.feedback: This describes how the claims were made, not how opinion at home was moved.

answers.text: Photographs of Congolese children with their hands cut off were shown in lantern-slide lectures abroad.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Leopold claimed the Congo basin in 1884 through a private association that spoke of science and humanity.
answers.feedback: This describes how Leopold took the land, not how opinion changed.

answers.text: The Berlin conference of 1884 and 1885 recognized Leopold's Congo Free State without any Africans present.
answers.feedback: This describes a decision of the powers, not a push from public opinion.

questions.text:
Why did Japan change so quickly? Japan was a smaller country, with one language and a strong sense of itself. Its leaders had a clear choice: reform or be swallowed. China was vast, and its court was divided, still convinced of its own greatness, and struggling with rebellions.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Japan was a smaller country with one language and a strong sense of itself, which helped its leaders.
answers.feedback: This is only part of the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Every Asian country that met Western ships was forced to reform at once or be swallowed up by them.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage compares two countries and does not describe every country.

answers.text: Japan was small, united, and forced to choose, while China was vast and divided.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: China reformed faster than Japan because its court was united and sure of its own greatness.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says China's court was divided and still convinced of its greatness.

questions.text:
Lin's seizure turned a quarrel between merchants and officials into a quarrel between governments. The British trade superintendent at Canton, Captain Charles Elliot, persuaded the merchants to hand over their opium by promising that the British government would pay for it. Once he had made that promise, the loss became a debt that only Parliament could settle, and the merchants had every reason to ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: ask London to send a fleet to settle the matter and pay the debt.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: stop trading at Canton until the Qing emperor had apologized.
answers.feedback: Nothing in the passage suggests the merchants would give up trade and wait for an apology.

answers.text: pay the debt among themselves, since only merchants had lost anything.
answers.feedback: The passage says the loss became a debt that only Parliament could settle.

answers.text: forget the loss quietly, since Elliot had already paid them back in full.
answers.feedback: The passage says Elliot only promised that the British government would pay.

questions.text:
The general staffs of every great power drew up war plans, and the plans made war more likely. Germany's Schlieffen Plan assumed a war against both France and Russia. It called for knocking out France in about six weeks by marching through neutral Belgium, then turning east to meet the slower Russians. Russia would take weeks to bring its army to the border by mobilization, and so the Germans could not wait. France had its own plan to attack in the east. All the plans depended on speed, and each country's mobilization looked like an act of war to its neighbors.

According to the text, why did the Germans feel they could not wait?

answers.text: Russia would take weeks to mobilize, so Germany had to knock out France in six weeks first.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: France would take weeks to mobilize, so Germany had to defeat Russia in six weeks first.
answers.feedback: This reverses the plan. The text says Russia was the slower of the two.

answers.text: Britain would blockade Germany within weeks, so Germany had to seize French ports quickly.
answers.feedback: The text does not mention a blockade in this passage.

answers.text: Belgium would join France within weeks, so Germany had to strike before its army was ready.
answers.feedback: The text says Germany planned to march through neutral Belgium, not to fight an ally of France there.

questions.text:
Once the order to mobilize was given, the trains would roll on a schedule that could not easily be stopped, rerouted, or improvised. A diplomat who asked for one more day of talks was asking the generals to put a finished machine into reverse.

Which choice best supports the idea that the German war plan could not easily be stopped once it began?

answers.text: In 1905 Kaiser Wilhelm landed at Tangier and spoke in favor of Moroccan independence, hoping to split Britain from France.
answers.feedback: This is a fact about a crisis in Morocco, not about the rigidity of the plan.

answers.text: Admiral Tirpitz hoped that a German fleet would make Britain think twice before it attacked.
answers.feedback: This describes the naval race and has nothing to do with the army's schedule.

answers.text: Moltke told the Kaiser that an army planned for years to go west could not be turned east in a night.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: In 1904 Britain reached an entente with France, and in 1907 it reached another with Russia.
answers.feedback: This describes the alliances, not the schedule of the German trains.

questions.text:
Neither side could find a way through. The generals tried longer bombardments, poison gas, which the Germans first used at Ypres in April 1915, and eventually tanks and aircraft. Still, they tended to fall back on attrition, the plan of wearing down the enemy until he broke. In February 1916 the Germans attacked the fortress of Verdun, expecting to bleed France white. The French held, under General Philippe Pétain, and the battle dragged on for ten months. In July 1916 the British attacked along the Somme. On the first day alone, nearly sixty thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. By November the combined losses on the Somme were over a million, and the line had moved only a few miles.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: On the first day of the Somme alone, nearly sixty thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded.
answers.feedback: This is one detail in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Neither side found a way through the trenches, and attrition cost enormous numbers of lives.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Modern weapons always make an attacking army lose far more men than the defending army does.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage describes one war and does not state a rule about all wars.

answers.text: The new weapons of gas, tanks, and aircraft quickly gave the attackers a decisive advantage.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says neither side could find a way through.

questions.text:
Even if a few men broke into the first trench, they had left their guns and supply carts behind them, while the defenders could bring up ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: tanks by river barge.
answers.feedback: Nothing in the passage mentions tanks or barges as a means of defense here.

answers.text: supplies from the enemy depots.
answers.feedback: The passage says the attackers, not the defenders, had left their supplies behind.

answers.text: guns by the roads the attackers had used.
answers.feedback: The passage says the defenders had the advantage of railways, not the attackers' roads.

answers.text: fresh reserves by railway.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

questions.text:
Article 231, the so-called war guilt clause, said Germany and its allies were responsible for the war and its damage. On that basis, Germany owed reparations, which a commission set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks, a huge sum.

According to the text, what did Article 231 say?

answers.text: Germany alone had started the war and must give up all of its colonies.
answers.feedback: The text says Germany and its allies were responsible, and it lists the colonies as a separate loss.

answers.text: Germany and its allies were responsible for the war and for its damage.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: The Allies shared responsibility with Germany for the cost of the war.
answers.feedback: This reverses the clause, which put the responsibility on Germany and its allies.

answers.text: Germany must pay reparations of 132 billion gold marks within one year.
answers.feedback: The text says a commission set that sum in 1921, and it does not give a deadline of one year.

questions.text:
A civil war between the Reds and the Whites, a mixed group of officers, liberals, and monarchists, lasted until 1921. The Whites were divided and had no common cause, while the Reds held the central cities and railways. Britain, France, the United States, and Japan sent troops at various times, but not enough to matter.

Which choice best supports the idea that the Reds had advantages that helped them win the civil war?

answers.text: Trotsky built the Red Army from volunteers and conscripts and drafted former tsarist officers.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: In 1921 sailors at Kronstadt, once heroes of the revolution, rose against the Bolsheviks and were crushed.
answers.feedback: This describes a revolt against the Bolsheviks, not an advantage in the war with the Whites.

answers.text: Lenin retreated from the harshest policies and allowed small private trade under the New Economic Policy.
answers.feedback: This describes a policy after the fighting, not an advantage in the war.

answers.text: In 1922 the Bolsheviks proclaimed the new Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in the lands they held.
answers.feedback: This describes what the Bolsheviks did after the war, not an advantage during it.

questions.text:
The republic also had a hidden weakness in its constitution. Its president had the power to issue emergency decrees under a clause called Article 48, which meant that a government unable to win a majority in parliament could still rule, as long as the president agreed. And with many small parties, no government held a firm majority for long. ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: Governments therefore rarely needed the president's approval to pass any law at all.
answers.feedback: The passage says a government without a majority could rule only if the president agreed.

answers.text: Governments therefore usually lasted for many years under one strong governing party.
answers.feedback: The passage says no government held a firm majority for long.

answers.text: Governments therefore had to rely on the army to carry out each emergency decree.
answers.feedback: The passage ties the decrees to the president, and it does not mention the army.

answers.text: Governments therefore often had to rule on the president's emergency decrees alone.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

questions.text:
The Ukrainian famine shows how the system worked. Quotas for grain were set so high that peasants had nothing left, and the villages that fell short were punished by having food and goods taken away. In January 1933 the government closed the borders of Ukraine and the nearby Kuban region to travelers, so that starving peasants could not leave in search of bread. The Great Purge began after the murder of a popular party leader, Sergei Kirov, in December 1934. At the show trials, old comrades of Lenin confessed and were shot. In 1937 the purge reached the Red Army, and most of its top officers were removed or killed. Within a few years Stalin had cleared the party of nearly every man who remembered a Russia without him.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Grain quotas were set so high that villages that fell short had food and goods taken away from them.
answers.feedback: This is one part of the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Every communist government has used famine and purges to control its own people and its rivals alike.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage describes the Soviet Union under Stalin.

answers.text: Stalin's government used quotas, closed borders, and purges to bring peasants and party under control.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: The Great Purge ended once it reached the Red Army, since its top officers all escaped removal or death.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says most of the top officers were removed or killed.

questions.text:
Chamberlain's reasons were not foolish. Britain's army was small, its air defenses were incomplete, and the public did not want war. Yet the choice had a cost. Czechoslovakia lost its mountain defenses, and in March 1939 Hitler took the rest of the country. This broke his promise and showed that his aims went beyond Germans living outside Germany. Britain and France now promised to defend Poland, which was clearly Hitler's next target. Some historians argue that war in 1938 would have found Germany weaker and the Allies better placed. Others reply that Britain and its dominions were not ready, and that the delay gave them time to build fighter planes and radar. Think about both claims as you prepare for this week's discussion.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Czechoslovakia lost its mountain defenses, and in March 1939 Hitler took the rest of the country.
answers.feedback: This is one consequence in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Giving in to an aggressor always makes war more likely and never buys time to prepare.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and it contradicts the passage, which says delay gave time for planes and radar.

answers.text: Munich cost Czechoslovakia its defenses and bought Britain time, and historians dispute its wisdom.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Chamberlain's reasons were foolish, since Britain's army and air defenses were fully ready.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says his reasons were not foolish and Britain was not ready.

questions.text:
The French had the Maginot Line, a chain of strong forts along the German border, and a large army. The Germans went around it. They sent tanks through the Ardennes, a hilly forest that French planners had judged too difficult for armor. The tanks reached the English Channel in ten days and trapped the British and some French forces at Dunkirk.

Which choice best supports the idea that France was poorly prepared for a German thrust through the Ardennes?

answers.text: Paris fell on June 14, and France signed an armistice at Compiègne on June 22.
answers.feedback: This describes the result of the defeat, not how well France was prepared.

answers.text: Churchill told Parliament on June 4 that wars are not won by evacuations, though over 330,000 men were taken off the beaches.
answers.feedback: This is a comment on Dunkirk, not on French preparation.

answers.text: General de Gaulle broadcast from London on June 18 that the war was not lost, and Vichy ruled the south.
answers.feedback: This describes events after the defeat, not French preparation.

answers.text: The French kept their best troops in the north and left their reserves thin behind them.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

questions.text:
The Nuremberg Laws defined a Jew by ancestry, not by belief. A person with three or four Jewish grandparents counted as a Jew, even if that person had been baptized as a Christian or had never set foot in a synagogue.

According to the text, how did the Nuremberg Laws define a Jew?

answers.text: By ancestry: a person with three or four Jewish grandparents counted as a Jew.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: By belief: anyone who attended a synagogue counted as a Jew under the law.
answers.feedback: The text says the laws defined a Jew by ancestry, not by belief.

answers.text: By residence: anyone who lived in a Jewish quarter of a city counted as a Jew.
answers.feedback: The text gives ancestry, not residence, as the test.

answers.text: By baptism: only those who had never been baptized as Christians counted as Jews.
answers.feedback: The text says a baptized person with Jewish grandparents still counted as a Jew.

questions.text:
On the morning of July 13, 1942, in the Polish village of Józefów, their commander told them that they were to round up the Jews of the village and shoot most of them, and he offered to excuse anyone who did not want to take part. Only about a dozen of nearly five hundred men stepped out at first. ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: Most of the men therefore refused as soon as they heard what the commander asked.
answers.feedback: The passage says only about a dozen of nearly five hundred men stepped out.

answers.text: Most of the men therefore took part although they had been told they could refuse.

answers.text: Most of the men therefore were hardened soldiers who had fought in the earlier war.
