questions.text:
Each side feared the other, and each had reasons. The Soviets remembered the German invasion that had killed some twenty-seven million of their people, and they saw Western strength as a threat. The Americans saw a government that ruled by force at home and appeared to seek more power abroad. Neither side could easily tell defense from aggression. A single misreading could harden suspicion into hostility, and in these years many did.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: The Soviets remembered a German invasion that had killed some twenty-seven million of their own people.
answers.feedback: This is one detail in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Great powers that fought as allies always become bitter enemies as soon as their war is over.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage describes one pair of powers.

answers.text: The Americans feared the Soviets only because they did not understand how weak the Soviet army was.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which gives each side real reasons for its fear.

answers.text: Both the Soviets and the Americans had real reasons to fear each other and could misread each other.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
The most dangerous moment came in October 1962. Fidel Castro, who had taken power in Cuba and turned it toward communism, accepted Soviet nuclear missiles on the island, only ninety miles from Florida. When American spy planes found them, Kennedy chose a naval quarantine instead of an air strike and demanded that the missiles be removed. For thirteen days the world held its breath. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev finally agreed to withdraw them, and in secret Kennedy agreed to ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: recognize Castro's government as the lawful government of Cuba.
answers.feedback: The passage mentions no such recognition.

answers.text: withdraw American troops from West Berlin at once.
answers.feedback: The passage mentions no withdrawal from Berlin.

answers.text: remove American missiles from Turkey as part of the bargain.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: pay the Soviet Union for the missiles it had removed.
answers.feedback: The passage says Khrushchev withdrew them, and it mentions no payment.

questions.text:
The Hungarian rising began on October 23, 1956, when students in Budapest read out their demands, and it spread quickly. Imre Nagy, a communist who had promised reform, became prime minister and announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. On November 4 Soviet tanks attacked the city. About 2,500 Hungarians and several hundred Soviet soldiers died, and some 200,000 Hungarians fled. Nagy was executed in 1958. The West protested but did not act, and its attention was on a crisis at Suez in Egypt. In August 1968 some two hundred thousand Warsaw Pact troops entered Czechoslovakia in a single night, and Dubcek was taken to Moscow. The Czechs, who had no hope of winning, mostly resisted without weapons.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: About 2,500 Hungarians and several hundred Soviet soldiers died when Soviet tanks attacked the city.
answers.feedback: This is one detail in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Soviet forces crushed the risings in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 as the West held back.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Popular uprisings in Eastern Europe in the 1950s and 1960s all succeeded in removing communist rulers.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, where the Soviets put both risings down.

answers.text: The Western powers sent troops and arms to help the Hungarians resist the Soviet tanks in Budapest.
answers.feedback: This contradicts the passage, which says the West protested but did not act.

questions.text:
The system brought some real gains. Illiteracy fell, and the Soviet Union produced rockets, scientists, and in 1957 the first artificial satellite, Sputnik. But planners could not know what millions of people wanted. Factories met their quotas by making goods nobody needed, and shops had long lines and empty shelves.

Which choice best supports the claim that planners could not know what people wanted?

answers.text: In East Germany a family might wait ten years or more for a small car, and apartments went by list.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Stalin died in March 1953, and in 1956 Khrushchev described his crimes in a secret speech.
answers.feedback: This describes a change of leaders, not what planners knew about demand.

answers.text: In 1985 the party chose a younger man, Mikhail Gorbachev, who believed the failing system could be fixed.
answers.feedback: This describes a later change of leader, not what planners knew about demand.

answers.text: In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, which shocked Americans.
answers.feedback: This describes a success in rockets, which does not show what planners knew about demand.

questions.text:
Gandhi taught satyagraha, the refusal to obey unjust laws without using violence, and he called the goal swaraj. He dressed in homespun cloth, lived simply, and drew millions of villagers into the cause. In 1930 he led a march of some 240 miles to the sea to make salt in defiance of the British tax on it. Tens of thousands were jailed.

According to the text, what did Gandhi's march of some 240 miles to the sea defy?

answers.text: The British government's tax on making salt.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: A British ban on wearing homespun cloth.
answers.feedback: The text says Gandhi himself wore homespun cloth. It names the salt tax as the target.

answers.text: The law that kept Indians out of the civil service.
answers.feedback: The text names the tax on salt as the law he defied by making salt.

answers.text: The order that had put India into the war.
answers.feedback: The text does not tie the march to that order.

questions.text:
Gandhi's method depended on an opponent who could be shamed by the sight of suffering. The British, having a free press and a conscience of their own, could be moved in this way.

Which choice best supports the idea that Gandhi's method worked on an opponent who could be shamed?

answers.text: In 1942 Sir Stafford Cripps offered self-government after the war, but Congress would not accept it.
answers.feedback: This describes a failed offer, not how a nonviolent march affected opinion.

answers.text: Police at Dharasana struck down marchers who raised no hand, and a reporter's account was printed abroad.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a lawyer who had once worked with Congress, came to demand a separate Muslim homeland.
answers.feedback: This describes a political demand, not how Gandhi's method shamed an opponent.

answers.text: Radcliffe was given a few weeks to draw the new borders through Punjab and Bengal without having seen India.
answers.feedback: This describes how partition was drawn, not how the method shamed an opponent.

questions.text:
The land called Palestine lay in the Ottoman Empire for four hundred years. Most of its people were Arab Muslims, with Christian Arabs and a small Jewish community. For Jews it was the ancient homeland, the land of David and the Temple, from which their ancestors had been exiled by Rome, and toward which they had prayed for nearly two thousand years. For Arabs it was the home in which their families had lived for generations.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: The land called Palestine lay in the Ottoman Empire for four hundred years before the First World War.
answers.feedback: This is one detail in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Two peoples with ties to one piece of land will always end up fighting over who owns it.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and the passage does not claim a rule about such cases.

answers.text: Most of the people of Palestine were Jews, with a small Arab community living among them.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says most of the people were Arab Muslims.

answers.text: Both Jews and Arabs had deep ties to the land of Palestine, each for reasons of their own.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
In 1922 about one person in ten in Palestine was Jewish. By 1939 it was nearly one in three. The Arab revolt began with a general strike in 1936, and Britain sent a commission under Lord Peel to find a way out. In 1937 the Peel Commission became the first to propose dividing the land into a Jewish state and an Arab state, and Arab leaders rejected the plan. The White Paper of 1939 chose another course: it limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years, after which any more would need ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: the approval of the British cabinet.
answers.feedback: The passage says the White Paper tied further immigration to Arab consent.

answers.text: a vote of the United Nations.
answers.feedback: The passage gives no role to the United Nations in this limit.

answers.text: the consent of the Arab leaders.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: the permission of the Jewish Agency.
answers.feedback: The passage gives no role to the Jewish Agency in this limit.

questions.text:
In October 1979 President Jimmy Carter allowed the exiled Shah to enter the United States for medical treatment. Many Iranians feared a repeat of 1953. On November 4, students stormed the American embassy in Tehran and seized more than sixty Americans. Khomeini backed them. Fifty-two of the hostages were held for 444 days, released only on the day Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981.

According to the text, how long were fifty-two of the hostages held?

answers.text: 52 days, until an American rescue attempt succeeded.
answers.feedback: The text says the rescue attempt failed.

answers.text: 444 days, until President Carter agreed to return the Shah.
answers.feedback: The text says they were released on the day Reagan took office.

answers.text: 444 days, until the very day Ronald Reagan took office.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: Fourteen months, until Khomeini died and his system ended.
answers.feedback: The text gives 444 days and the day Reagan took office. Khomeini lived until 1989.

questions.text:
Many religious Iranians were angered by his Western ways, and many bazaar merchants and students resented his power. His alliance with America made the United States a target of their anger.

Which choice best supports the idea that the Shah's alliance with America made the United States a target?

answers.text: A 1953 plot backed by the CIA removed Mossadegh, after which the Shah ruled with American backing.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: The Shah's White Revolution of the 1960s gave land to peasants and the vote to women.
answers.feedback: This describes his reforms, not how America became a target.

answers.text: In 1971 the Shah held a great celebration at Persepolis for guests from around the world.
answers.feedback: This describes a display of wealth, not America's role.

answers.text: After 1973 oil prices quadrupled, Iran's income soared, and millions of villagers moved to the cities.
answers.feedback: This describes an economic change, not America's role.

questions.text:
Before it, cargo was loaded piece by piece, in sacks, barrels, and crates carried aboard by gangs of dockworkers, and a ship could sit in port for days. McLean's own figures put the cost of loading a ton at about six dollars by the old method and about sixteen cents by container.

According to the text, what was the cost of loading a ton by container, by McLean's own figures?

answers.text: About six dollars.
answers.feedback: The text gives six dollars as the cost by the old method.

answers.text: About sixteen cents.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: About sixty cents.
answers.feedback: The text gives sixteen cents for the container.

answers.text: About sixteen dollars.
answers.feedback: The text gives sixteen cents, not sixteen dollars.

questions.text:
Schuman did not promise a united Europe at once. "Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single plan," he said. It would be built, he went on, through concrete achievements that first created ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: an army under French command.
answers.feedback: The passage says Schuman did not promise a united Europe at once, and it does not mention an army.

answers.text: a currency used by every member.
answers.feedback: The passage describes the coal and steel community, not a currency.

answers.text: a constitution for the continent.
answers.feedback: The passage says Europe would not be made all at once or by a single plan.

answers.text: a solidarity among the peoples.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

questions.text:
Read the passage below. Then answer the ten questions that follow it.

1  Robert Owen, a Welshman who rose from shop boy to mill manager, took over the cotton mills at New Lanark, in Scotland, in 1800. The mills had belonged to his father-in-law, David Dale. Owen cut the working day, refused to hire young children, built a school, opened a shop that sold decent goods at fair prices, and cleaned up the village. He even hung a small four-colored block over each worker's machine, turned to a color that showed how well that worker had behaved that day, so that managers did not have to scold. Visitors came from across Europe to see the result. The mills still made a profit. Owen pressed Parliament for a law to protect children in the mills, and an act passed in 1819, though it was weakly enforced. Owen argued that people are shaped by their surroundings and that good surroundings would make good workers. If surroundings alone make a person's character, though, there is little room left for choice and virtue. Ask yourself whether that is true.

2  By about 1816 Owen had opened a building he called the New Institution for the Formation of Character, with a school for the youngest children, who were taught through play, song, and dancing rather than the rod. The village held around two thousand people, and the mill's working day had been cut to about ten and a half hours. Grand Duke Nicholas of Russia, later Tsar Nicholas I, was among the visitors who came to see it.

3  Later Owen grew bolder. He believed a whole society could be built on shared property and cooperation, and he started a community at New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825. It broke up within a few years. His followers were among the first to be called socialists, and the word socialism began to spread.

4  The third thinker was Karl Marx, a German philosopher born in 1818. Exiled for his writings, he settled in London, where he spent his days reading in the British Museum and lived much of his life in poverty. His friend Friedrich Engels, whose family owned a cotton mill in Manchester, had written a harsh account of the workers' lives there, and Engels's income from the mill helped to support Marx. Together they published The Communist Manifesto in 1848, for a small group of exiled workers, and few people read it at the time. Its famous opening claim was that the history of all society was the history of class struggle. In the English translation of 1888 the sentence reads, "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." In modern times, Marx said, it was a struggle between the bourgeoisie, who owned the factories and the capital, and the proletariat, who sold their labor for wages. He predicted that the workers would one day rise up, seize the factories, and end private ownership altogether, ending in a classless society. Marx spent the rest of his life on a long study of the economy, Capital, whose first volume appeared in 1867, and he died in London in 1883.

5  The heart of Capital was an argument about wages. A worker, Marx said, creates more value in a day than he is paid for, and the owner keeps the difference as profit. The more machines the owner installs, the more he can squeeze from each worker, and the wider the gap between owners and workers grows. Many economists later argued that this theory misjudged how wages and prices are set, and wages did rise over the century instead of falling. Still, the question he asked was hard to dismiss. Why did the gains of one side so often look like the losses of the other?

6  Marx wrote with real force, and he drew attention to real hardships. But judge his argument as you would any other. He claimed that economic conditions drive nearly everything else, and that ideas, religion, and law are only reflections of them. Yet the factory laws you just read about came partly from ideas, since they were driven by Christian conscience and public argument. He also predicted that workers in the most industrial country would rebel first. Britain's workers did not. Their wages rose, their unions grew, and Parliament widened the vote.
According to the passage, how long was the working day at New Lanark by about 1816?

answers.text: About eight hours a day.
answers.feedback: The passage says the day had been cut to about ten and a half hours, not eight.

answers.text: About twelve hours a day.
answers.feedback: The passage says Owen had cut the day below the usual long workday.

answers.text: About ten and a half hours.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate the part of the passage the question names, then match it to what the passage states.

answers.text: About fourteen hours a day.
answers.feedback: The passage gives about ten and a half hours.

questions.text: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word squeeze most nearly means

answers.text: draw out.
answers.feedback: Correct. Put each choice into the sentence in place of the word and keep the one that preserves the sentence's meaning.

answers.text: press tightly.
answers.feedback: This fits the word's physical sense, but a person cannot press profit tightly out of a worker.

answers.text: hug.
answers.feedback: This is another physical sense, and it makes no sense with profit and workers.

answers.text: crowd into.
answers.feedback: This is a different sense, and it does not fit the idea of taking more profit from a worker.

questions.text: Which choice best describes the author's attitude toward Marx's argument about wages, as paragraphs 5 and 6 present it?

answers.text: Dismissive, because the author thinks the argument was entirely mistaken and worthless to consider.
answers.feedback: The author calls the question hard to dismiss, so the attitude is not dismissive.

answers.text: Enthusiastic, because the author thinks history proved the argument correct in every respect it made.
answers.feedback: The author says wages did rise instead of falling, so history did not prove it right.

answers.text: Indifferent, because the author only mentions the argument and takes no view of it, one way or the other.
answers.feedback: The author notes economists' criticism and calls the question hard to dismiss, which shows a view.

answers.text: Measured: it takes the question seriously while noting that many economists found the theory flawed.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find the words that carry judgment, then match both the direction and the strength of the attitude.

questions.text: In paragraph 1, the detail about the four-colored block over each worker's machine mainly serves to

answers.text: prove that Owen's methods cost more than the mills could earn.
answers.feedback: The passage says the mills still made a profit.

answers.text: show an unusual way Owen guided behavior without scolding anyone.
answers.feedback: Correct. Ask what job the detail does for the paragraph, not just what it is about.

answers.text: explain why visitors came from across Europe to dislike his mills.
answers.feedback: The passage says visitors came to see the result, and it does not say they disliked it.

answers.text: show that the workers chose their own hours of work each day.
answers.feedback: The passage says the block showed how well each worker had behaved.

questions.text: The passage most strongly suggests that the author

answers.text: agrees fully that good surroundings will always produce good workers.
answers.feedback: The author says that if surroundings alone made character, there would be little room for choice and virtue.

answers.text: believes that Owen's mills failed because their workers were too well treated.
answers.feedback: The passage says the mills still made a profit.

answers.text: doubts that surroundings alone make a person's character or decide his virtue.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find what the passage establishes, then choose the answer that needs the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: thinks that virtue is something that no school or community can ever teach.
answers.feedback: The passage does not say this. It raises a doubt about one view of character.

questions.text: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

answers.text: It describes Owen's mill and community, then Marx's life and claims, and closes with a criticism.
answers.feedback: Correct. Say in a few words what each part does, then match the movement of the passage to the choice.

answers.text: It presents Marx's argument first and then shows how Owen's mill proved it true in practice, step by step.
answers.feedback: The passage takes Owen first, and it does not say his mill proved anything about Marx.

answers.text: It compares Owen and Marx point by point on wages, schools, and property in alternating paragraphs throughout.
answers.feedback: The passage treats each man in turn and does not alternate between them.

answers.text: It argues step by step that Owen's ideas were better than Marx's and ought to have been adopted widely.
answers.feedback: The passage describes both men and does not rank them or argue for either.

questions.text: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

answers.text: Owen's mills at New Lanark made a profit while treating their workers with decency, schooling, and care.
answers.feedback: This is one detail from the first paragraph, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

answers.text: Reformers of the 1800s all believed that private ownership of property ought to be ended in every country.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and it distorts the passage, since Owen began as a mill manager.

answers.text: Owen and Marx agreed that a revolution by the workers was both certain and desirable to them both.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which gives Marx the prediction of a rising and does not give it to Owen.

answers.text: Owen and Marx gave two different responses to industrial hardship, each with flaws the passage notes.
answers.feedback: Correct. Read the whole passage, separate the central point from the examples, and reject choices that are too narrow, too broad, or distorted.

questions.text: According to Marx's argument as paragraph 5 presents it, what follows when an owner installs more machines?

answers.text: The gap between owners and workers grows narrower, because the machines do the work for all.
answers.feedback: This reverses the direction. The passage says the gap widens with more machines.

answers.text: The owner can squeeze more from each worker, and the gap between owners and workers widens.
answers.feedback: Correct. Name the relationship, find both ends in the passage, and check which event causes which.

answers.text: The workers earn more value for their labor, because machines make each worker more skilled.
answers.feedback: The passage says the owner keeps the difference between value created and pay.

answers.text: The owner needs fewer workers, so the remaining workers share the profit among themselves.
answers.feedback: The passage says the owner keeps the difference as profit, not the workers.

questions.text: Based on the passage, which situation would Marx most likely cite as an example of class struggle?

answers.text: Factory workers sell their labor for wages while the owner keeps the profit they produce.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find the principle the passage shows, restate it, and test each choice against the passage's own logic.

answers.text: A village where all families share the property and cooperate equally in their daily work.
answers.feedback: This describes the kind of community Owen tried to build, not a struggle between classes.

answers.text: A merchant who sells cloth at fair prices to every customer who comes to his shop.
answers.feedback: This describes fair trade, not a struggle between owners and workers.

answers.text: Visitors who tour a mill to learn how a manager treats the workers who run its machines.
answers.feedback: This describes interest in a mill, not a struggle between owners and workers.

questions.text: According to the passage, where did Marx spend his days reading after he settled in London?

answers.text: In Engels's cotton mill in Manchester.
answers.feedback: The passage says Engels's family owned the mill and that its income helped to support Marx.

answers.text: In a lecture hall at a university in Berlin.
answers.feedback: The passage says Marx was exiled and living in London.

answers.text: In the library of the British Museum.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate the part of the passage the question names, then match it to what the passage states.

answers.text: In the library of the House of Commons.
answers.feedback: The passage names the British Museum.

questions.text: In a few sentences, describe the test-taking strategy you used on this exam. What did you do first, and how did you decide between answer choices?

Final question: record your answer.

Record a single video of about five minutes that answers all three questions below, one after another, in your own words. Speak in your own voice and do not read from a script. You may glance at brief notes, but each answer must explain the connections yourself, using at least two examples from the passages in this exam. You can record on a phone, a tablet, or a computer. Then upload that one video file here. Do not upload more than one file.

  1. Choose two turning points from this exam where a single leader’s decision seems to have mattered. For each, explain what larger forces were already pushing events and how far the leader’s choice still changed the outcome.
  2. The passage about Owen and Marx shows two answers to the hardships of industry. Using that passage and at least one example of the Soviet Union from this exam, explain how an idea about fairness for workers could lead to very different results depending on who held power.
  3. Several systems in this exam looked strong from the top but depended on something their leaders ignored or hid. Choose two, such as the German war plan, the Treaty of Versailles, the Soviet planned economy, or British rule in India, and explain what each depended on and what happened when that support failed.

quizzes.title: Semester Final Exam: Weeks 19 to 36
quizzes.description:
SEMESTER FINAL EXAM
The Modern World
56 questions · 55 points · one attempt
◉ ◌ ◉
About this exam

This exam covers the whole semester. It has 55 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. Five of them begin with a short passage from the lessons. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

Before you start

Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you start. Then choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: The lesson doubts the story that Moctezuma took Cortés for a returning god. What is the main reason?

answers.text: The story comes mostly from sources written after the conquest.
Moctezuma never met Cortés before the Spaniards entered the city.
The Mexica had no gods who were said to return from the east.
Cortés wrote that Moctezuma had refused to speak with him at all.

questions.feedback_correct: A simpler explanation is more likely: Moctezuma was curious, cautious, and unsure what the strangers wanted.

questions.text: How did the civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa help Pizarro?

answers.text: Huáscar sent his own army to join the Spaniards against his brother.
The Inca had given up their roads and left the mountains undefended.
The armies were worn out, and the best generals had been lost.
Atahualpa had already agreed to pay tribute to the king of Spain.

questions.feedback_correct: Pizarro arrived as the war ended. A year earlier he would have met a united empire.

questions.text: Why could even the silver of Peru and Mexico not solve Philip II's money troubles?

answers.text: The silver ships were seized by Dutch pirates before they reached Spain.
The Crown gave all of the silver to the Church, which spent it on buildings.
The silver lost its value when the Dutch began to make coins from tin.
He fought the Turks and the Dutch rebels, and the bills were too large.

questions.feedback_correct: His government went bankrupt in 1575, and his unpaid soldiers mutinied.

questions.text: What did the Dutch East India Company do in the Banda Islands in 1621?

answers.text: It signed a treaty that let the islanders sell nutmeg to any buyer they chose.
It killed or enslaved most islanders to enforce its nutmeg monopoly.
It gave the islands to the Dutch government in return for a large payment.
It built a port at Batavia and left the islanders to govern themselves.

questions.feedback_correct: The islanders had refused to sell only to the Dutch. The monopoly was enforced by arms as well as by contract.

questions.text: The Taíno nearly vanished from the Caribbean within two generations of Columbus's arrival. What was the chief cause?

answers.text: Spanish armies killed most of them in open battle on the larger islands.
Most of them left for the mainland, where they merged with other peoples.
Diseases they had never met, with forced labor adding to the toll.
A famine that followed when Spanish cattle destroyed their fields.

questions.feedback_correct: The Spaniards did not understand what was happening, and they did not intend it.

questions.text: What does the letter of Afonso I of Kongo to the king of Portugal show?

answers.text: The slave trade was criticized from the start, including by African rulers.
The kings of Kongo were the largest sellers of captives on the West African coast.
The king of Portugal had agreed to stop the trade after his complaint.
Christian kings in Africa had no way to communicate with Europe.

questions.feedback_correct: Afonso wrote in 1526 that Portuguese merchants were kidnapping his people. The king of Portugal never stopped the trade.

questions.text: What did Puritan emigration in the 1630s do to England and to America?

answers.text: It ended the quarrel between Charles and Parliament over taxes.
It drained England of reformers and gave America Puritan roots.
It made the Puritans a small group with no voice in the Civil War.
It filled the new colonies with Catholics who had fled from Laud.

questions.feedback_correct: Thousands sailed across the Atlantic and founded colonies such as Massachusetts Bay.

questions.text: Why did the trial of the seven bishops in 1688 turn so many English people against James II?

answers.text: The bishops were found guilty of treason and the king had them executed.
The king proved that Parliament had no right to oppose him in court.
The jury was made up of Catholics who voted in favor of the bishops.
Many feared a king of divine right who might rule without Parliament.

questions.feedback_correct: A jury found the bishops not guilty, and London rang with celebration.

questions.text: Why did Louis XIV rely on intendants in the provinces?

answers.text: They were great nobles who had sworn an oath to defend the Church.
They were generals who commanded the armies of each province.
They were elected by the towns and answered to the local judges.
They were royal agents drawn from lawyers and townsmen, with no local power.

questions.feedback_correct: Because they had no local base, they depended on the king. They collected taxes, kept order, and recruited soldiers.

questions.text: What tax reform did Marshal Vauban propose, and how did Louis respond?

answers.text: A tax on all foreign trade. Louis accepted it and named Vauban a minister.
A fairer tax that nobles and clergy would also pay. Louis banned the book.
A tax on Versailles itself. Louis agreed and sold part of the palace.
A tax on the Church only. Louis rejected it because the pope objected.

questions.feedback_correct: Vauban died soon after. His plan went unused, and the problem he named stayed with France for the rest of the century.

questions.text: What was the Republic of Letters?

answers.text: A network of scholars across Europe who wrote in Latin and French.
A court in Paris that tried writers who published without the king's leave.
A group of kings who agreed to share the cost of printing the Encyclopédie.
A school in London where the sons of nobles were taught to read.

questions.feedback_correct: Learned societies such as the Royal Society in London and the Academy of Sciences in Paris helped. Cheaper printing did the rest.

questions.text: What cause did Voltaire take up in the case of Jean Calas?

answers.text: Free trade. He wrote a pamphlet against the tax on salt.
The social contract. He asked the king to give the people a constitution.
Toleration. He campaigned for three years to overturn the verdict.
The separation of powers. He wrote a book to praise the English judges.

questions.feedback_correct: Calas, a Protestant merchant, was executed in Toulouse on a false charge in 1762.

questions.text: Why did the Proclamation of 1763 anger many American colonists?

answers.text: It ordered them to pay for the French and Indian War out of their own savings.
It forbade settlement beyond the Appalachians, where many hoped to claim land.
It required every colonist to swear loyalty to the Church of England.
It taxed every colonist who wished to buy or sell goods in the thirteen colonies.

questions.feedback_correct: London meant to keep order on the frontier after Pontiac's rising, but keeping soldiers there cost money.

questions.text: A parlement in France could refuse to register a royal law. How did it differ from the British Parliament?

answers.text: It was an assembly of the clergy that met in the king's palace.
It was a council of the king's ministers that could not refuse his orders.
It was a group of generals that decided how taxes would be spent.
It was a high law court and not an elected assembly of the people.

questions.feedback_correct: In 1788 the parlement of Paris said that only the Estates-General could approve the new taxes.

questions.text: Why did the flight to Varennes damage the Constitution of 1791?

answers.text: The king had taken the army with him and had declared war on France.
The Assembly learned that the king had signed a treaty with the pope.
Most people believed the king had tried to desert the Revolution.
The royal family had reached the frontier and left France for good.

questions.feedback_correct: A constitution that depended on the king's honest cooperation lost its foundation. The family was brought back from Varennes.

questions.text: What happened on the ninth of Thermidor?

answers.text: Deputies shouted Robespierre down, and he was executed the next day.
Robespierre dissolved the Convention and made himself the ruler of France.
The army marched on Paris and put the Committee of Public Safety on trial.
The Paris city government freed Robespierre and put the Convention to flight.

questions.feedback_correct: The Terror ended, though not at once. Prisoners were freed, the Jacobin club was closed, and the Directory took power in 1795.

questions.text: What saved Napoleon at Saint-Cloud during the coup of Brumaire?

answers.text: The army of the Directory refused to fire on its own commander.
The deputies voted to give him power after hearing his speech.
Lucien told the soldiers the deputies had tried to stab Napoleon.
Sieyès arrested the leaders of the councils before they could act.

questions.feedback_correct: The troops cleared the hall. The lesson says a few steadier nerves in the hall might have left Napoleon an exile or a prisoner.

questions.text: How did yellow fever change the map of the Americas around 1803?

answers.text: It killed Toussaint Louverture, and Haiti became a French colony again.
It killed most French soldiers in Haiti, and Napoleon sold Louisiana.
It spread among the Spanish troops and let Bolívar free Venezuela.
It ended the war between France and Britain, and Louisiana was left to Spain.

questions.feedback_correct: Haiti declared its independence in 1804. A disease had changed the map.

questions.text: What bottleneck did inventors such as Hargreaves and Arkwright attack in the making of cloth?

answers.text: One spinner made one thread at a time, so weavers waited for yarn.
Cotton was too expensive to import, so mills lacked raw material.
Looms could not be powered by water, so weaving was done by hand.
Dyes were scarce, so cloth could not be sold outside Britain.

questions.feedback_correct: The spinning jenny, the water frame, the mule, and the power loom each answered a part of the problem.

questions.text: What did Robert Owen's mills at New Lanark show?

answers.text: Model communities of workers lasted for generations wherever he founded one.
Shorter hours and good schools cost so much that the mill lost money.
Hand labor was cheaper in the end than machines, so the mill dropped them.
A mill could treat its workers decently and still make a profit.

questions.feedback_correct: He cut the working day, refused to hire young children, built a school, and cleaned up the village. His later community at New Harmony broke up within a few years.

questions.text: What was the Concert of Europe?

answers.text: An agreement among the great powers to meet when trouble arose.
A treaty among Germany's states to make war against France together.
A pledge by the Christian kings to defend the pope in Rome.
A union of the Italian states under the king of Piedmont.

questions.feedback_correct: The Congress of Vienna was judged by the first test of any regime, which was whether it kept the peace. No great war engulfed Europe until 1854.

questions.text: Why did Napoleon III sign a sudden peace with Austria in 1859?

answers.text: He had been defeated at Solferino and could not continue the war.
He had received Venetia and Lombardy from Austria in return.
He had been asked by the pope to protect Rome from Piedmont.
He was alarmed by the cost and by the nationalism he had set loose.

questions.feedback_correct: Venetia remained in Austrian hands, and Cavour resigned in anger.

questions.text: What happened to the East India Company after the revolt of 1857?

answers.text: It was given the right to raise its own army from the Punjab.
It moved its capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
Parliament abolished it and put India directly under the Crown.
It was sold to the princes who had stayed loyal to Britain.

questions.feedback_correct: This was the Raj. In 1877 Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.

questions.text: What did the treaties of 1854 and 1858 do to Japan?

answers.text: They closed the ports of Japan to all Western ships for another century.
They opened ports to American trade on terms like those forced on China.
They gave Hokkaido to the United States as a naval base.
They made the emperor of Japan a servant of the American president.

questions.feedback_correct: The shogun's advisers were divided, and they knew the Chinese had already lost to the British.

questions.text: Why did Bismarck's alliance system come apart after 1890?

answers.text: It was ended by a vote of the German parliament in 1890.
It rested on one man, whom Wilhelm II dismissed in 1890.
It was undone when Italy joined the Triple Entente in 1894.
It collapsed when Britain declared war on Germany in 1890.

questions.feedback_correct: Russia and France then signed an alliance in 1894, and Germany had enemies on both sides.

questions.text: What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk do?

answers.text: It ended the war in the west and sent American troops home.
It made Russia a member of the Triple Entente again.
It gave Germany much Russian land and freed its armies.
It gave Poland to Austria and Finland to Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: Freed from the east, Germany tried a great offensive in the spring of 1918.

questions.text: What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles say?

answers.text: Germany must give up its colonies and its navy.
Germany would join the League of Nations at once.
Germany must return Alsace and Lorraine within a year.
Germany and its allies were responsible for the war.

questions.feedback_correct: On that basis Germany owed reparations, which a commission set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.

questions.text: What did Stalin's Great Purge do to the Communist Party?

answers.text: Show trials forced old Bolsheviks to confess, and many were shot.
It made the party larger by letting in workers and peasants.
It gave Trotsky the leadership of the party after Lenin.
It ended the Five-Year Plan and returned the land to the peasants.

questions.feedback_correct: Millions more went to the labor camps of the Gulag.

questions.text: Why was the surrender at Stalingrad a turning point?

answers.text: The United States entered the war after the Germans sank an American ship.
Hitler agreed to retreat and the Germans withdrew from Russia.
The Japanese attacked Siberia, and the Soviets made peace with Hitler.
A German army of 200,000 was lost, and the Soviets began to advance.

questions.feedback_correct: Hitler had forbidden retreat. The army surrendered in February 1943.

questions.text: What did the Nuremberg court hold about orders from a superior?

answers.text: That obedience to orders was no defense for such crimes.
That a soldier who obeyed an order could never be tried.
That only the Führer could be held to account for the war.
That orders given in wartime were outside the law.

questions.feedback_correct: Twelve defendants were sentenced to death. The word genocide had been coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944.

questions.text: What was the pledge of NATO in 1949?

answers.text: Members would share their atomic weapons with the Soviet Union.
An attack on one member was an attack on all.
Members would lend money to rebuild the countries of Eastern Europe.
Members would keep their armies out of Germany.

questions.feedback_correct: The Soviets formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955 with their satellites.

questions.text: What did the Brezhnev Doctrine declare?

answers.text: The Soviets would let each satellite state choose its own government.
The Soviets would reduce their armies if the West did the same.
The Soviets would act if socialism was threatened in a member state.
The Soviets would open the borders of Eastern Europe to trade.

questions.feedback_correct: Brezhnev sent Warsaw Pact troops into Czechoslovakia in 1968 after the Prague Spring.

questions.text: What did the Suez affair of 1956 show about Britain and France?

answers.text: They had won back control of the canal by their own power.
They could no longer act as great powers on their own.
They had forced the United States to side with them.
They had the full support of the Soviet Union.

questions.feedback_correct: The United States and the Soviet Union both demanded that they stop, and they withdrew.

questions.text: What did the Oslo Accords of 1993 create?

answers.text: A fully independent Palestinian state with its capital in Jerusalem.
A final peace treaty that settled all the borders of Israel.
A United Nations force to guard the holy places of Jerusalem.
A Palestinian Authority to govern parts of the West Bank and Gaza.

questions.feedback_correct: The hardest questions, such as borders, Jerusalem, refugees, and settlements, were left unsettled.

questions.text: Why did many Iranians resent the United States by 1979?

answers.text: It had sold weapons to Iraq before the war with Iran began.
It had invaded Iran to protect the oil fields in 1951.
It had helped remove Mossadegh in 1953 and backed the Shah.
It had made the Shah give up his throne in favor of Khomeini.

questions.feedback_correct: The Shah's alliance with America made the United States a target of anger.

questions.text: Why did the shipping container lower the cost of trade so sharply?

answers.text: A crate could pass from ship to train to truck unopened, so loading by hand mostly ended.
Ships sailed faster, so each cargo spent less time at sea.
Customs officers inspected each crate once, at the first port, and later ports charged less.
Ships were built of lighter metal, so each voyage burned less fuel.

questions.feedback_correct: Loading costs dropped sharply, and it became cheap to make goods far from where they were sold.

questions.text: Several lessons describe a small event that might have changed history, such as the Quebec cliff path, the hall at Saint-Cloud, and the wrong turn at Sarajevo. What does the course suggest?

answers.text: Great events always had one cause, and small events did not matter.
Historians can tell in advance which events will change the world.
Outcomes depended on particular choices and chances, not on fate.
Leaders had little power, since large forces decided everything.

questions.feedback_correct: The lessons repeatedly ask what would have happened if one person had chosen differently.

questions.text: Britain borrowed cheaply, the Dutch built a bourse, and the French kings paid higher interest. What do the lessons suggest about credit?

answers.text: States whose lenders trusted a parliament could borrow more cheaply.
States with the largest populations could always borrow the most.
States with a king could borrow more cheaply because he was always repaid.
States that held the most silver had no need to borrow at all.

questions.feedback_correct: Lenders trusted Parliament more than a king, and French kings had been known to delay or cancel debts.

questions.text: The Dutch tolerated several faiths, while Louis XIV drove out the Huguenots. What did each choice bring?

answers.text: The Dutch lost many skilled people, and Louis gained a united kingdom.
Both kingdoms grew richer, and both avoided war with their neighbors.
Neither choice had any effect on trade or on the strength of the state.
The Dutch gained skilled people, and Louis armed his rivals with them.

questions.feedback_correct: Tolerance in Amsterdam had good business sense in it. The Huguenots who fled included weavers, bankers, and army officers.

questions.text: What idea ties together Locke, the colonists who protested the Stamp Act, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man?

answers.text: A king may rule as he wishes if he is chosen by the Church.
Government rests on consent and must protect the people's rights.
Government should be run only by those who own the most land.
The people may never resist a government that keeps order.

questions.feedback_correct: Locke published his Treatises in 1689. The colonists replied that they could not be taxed without their consent.

questions.text: Montesquieu, Rousseau, Robespierre, and Bolívar all thought about what free government needs. What do the lessons conclude?

answers.text: Good laws need good habits, which force cannot create.
Good laws alone are enough to keep a people free.
A strong leader can teach virtue quickly through fear.
Habits matter little once a constitution is written.

questions.feedback_correct: Habits grow slowly through families, churches, and schools. Bolívar learned how hard it is to build free government without them.

questions.text: Louis XIV, Napoleon, Bismarck's Germany, and the Kaiser each led other powers to join against the strongest. What principle is this?

answers.text: The divine right of kings.
The separation of powers.
The balance of power.
The invisible hand.

questions.feedback_correct: When one state grows strong enough to dominate its neighbors, the others unite against it.

questions.text: Napoleon's armies, the revolutions of 1848, Italy, Germany, and Versailles all involved nationalism. What do the lessons show?

answers.text: It faded after the revolutions of 1848 failed and played little part in later wars.
It was powerful but hard to satisfy, since new borders left many minorities.
It matched states to peoples, so few minorities remained after 1919.
It served only the great powers, which used it to take land from weaker neighbors.

questions.feedback_correct: The shape of the new states depended on particular decisions. After 1919, millions were left in states ruled by another nation.

questions.text: Cortés, Clive, and the Europeans in Africa all used local people. What does this show about empire?

answers.text: Conquerors won only by the force of their own weapons.
Local people refused to take any part in the new governments.
Local rulers always gave way as soon as Europeans arrived.
Conquerors relied on local rivals, soldiers, and workers.

questions.feedback_correct: Native allies were most of Cortés's army, sepoys fought for the Company, and Africans did most of the work of building roads and railways.

questions.text: Smith, Marx, Stalin's Five-Year Plan, and the collapse of communism all concern who decides what is made. Which statement fits the lessons?

answers.text: Planners set prices well, but markets left too many workers without jobs.
Planned economies made more goods than markets, though at a cost in freedom.
Markets and plans did equally well, so the choice between them was one of taste.
Planners lacked price signals, while markets made wealth at some cost.

questions.feedback_correct: Planners could not know what millions wanted. The lesson on globalization notes that a worker whose job moves abroad may lose it.

questions.text: Napoleon, Lenin, Stalin, and Hitler each built a regime around one man or one party. What weakness do the lessons name?

answers.text: They gave so much power to parliaments that no ruler could act in a crisis.
They rested on one will and shut out peaceful ways to settle quarrels.
They fell within a few years, because the people rose against each of them.
They held power only by free elections, which each regime lost at last.

questions.feedback_correct: A free republic needs ways to settle quarrels peacefully, and the Terror had destroyed them.

questions.text: From the sugar plantation to Haiti to abolition, which statement fits the course?

answers.text: Sugar spread slavery, the enslaved resisted, and abolition took decades.
Sugar spread slavery, and abolition followed as soon as Haiti won independence.
Sugar became unprofitable, so planters freed the enslaved and Parliament agreed.
The enslaved had little part in ending slavery, which came from Parliament alone.

questions.feedback_correct: Haiti declared independence in 1804. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and abolished slavery in 1833.

questions.text: Spanish silver, Philip II's bankruptcies, and Louis XVI's debt show what about wealth and the state?

answers.text: Spain fell behind only because the Dutch captured its silver ships.
A state with good credit need not tax its people, since lenders will wait.
Treasure and loans cannot replace production and fair taxes.
Only states with no silver of their own ever fell deeply into debt.

questions.feedback_correct: A country gets rich by producing things, not by digging up money. France went bankrupt in 1789.

questions.text: The lessons warn against the old story that reason simply marched forward. Which evidence supports that warning?

answers.text: Every Enlightenment writer opposed kings, and no king read their works.
The Enlightenment reached nearly every peasant in Europe within a few years.
Its ideas served absolute monarchs as well as their challengers.
Enlightenment thinkers all agreed on how government should be run.

questions.feedback_correct: Frederick and Catherine used the ideas to reform from above, and revolutionaries later claimed to speak for the general will.

questions.text: Berlin drew Africa's borders, the League gave out mandates, and Radcliffe drew the line in Punjab and Bengal. What do the lessons say about borders drawn by outsiders?

answers.text: They usually matched the languages and customs of the people, with a few exceptions.
They were redrawn within a decade by the peoples themselves, with little conflict.
They mattered little once independence came, because the new states drew their own.
They often cut across peoples or joined enemies, leaving lasting problems.

questions.feedback_correct: The new states often inherited borders that cut across peoples and joined enemies, and many soon fell under one-party or military rule.

questions.text:
Hundreds of thousands of French soldiers were tied down in Spain for years. Napoleon later called it "the Spanish ulcer." The French army was strong in open battle, but its best tool, the swift campaign against a single enemy army, was useless against a whole population. A column that held a town did not hold the road beyond it. Couriers needed escorts, foragers disappeared, and every garrison had to be fed from a countryside that hated it. The British, who could be supplied by sea through Portuguese ports, always had somewhere to fall back to.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Britain won in Spain because its soldiers were better trained than the French.
answers.feedback: The passage says the British could be supplied by sea, not that their soldiers were better trained.

answers.text: Spanish farmers refused to feed French garrisons, and that alone ended Napoleon's rule.
answers.feedback: This is too extreme. The passage says supply troubles hurt the French but does not say they alone ended Napoleon's rule.

answers.text: The French army's strength in open battle did little good against a hostile population in Spain.
answers.feedback: It covers the whole passage: strength in open battle, and failure against a whole population.

answers.text: Napoleon lost soldiers in Spain mainly because couriers and foragers deserted.
answers.feedback: This changes a detail. The passage says foragers disappeared but never says anyone deserted.

questions.text:
Newton's ideas had to win over doubters, and they did it by measurement. Newton's theory said that the Earth bulges at the equator and is flatter at the poles. Many French scientists, who had followed Descartes, expected the opposite. In the 1730s the Academy of Sciences sent expeditions to Peru and to Lapland, in the far north of Europe, to measure the length of a degree of the Earth's curve.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: The results agreed with Newton's prediction, and doubters began to give way.
answers.feedback: The first sentence says Newton's ideas won by measurement, so the results must have favored him.

answers.text: The results were unclear, and French scientists kept to Descartes's view for another century.
answers.feedback: This contradicts the first sentence, which says measurement won over the doubters.

answers.text: The results agreed with the French scientists' expectation, and Newton's theory was set aside.
answers.feedback: This reverses the outcome. The passage says Newton's ideas won, not those of the French scientists.

answers.text: The Academy cancelled the expeditions after deciding that the question could not be settled by measurement.
answers.feedback: The passage says the expeditions were sent and that measurement did the persuading, so they were not cancelled.

questions.text:
The result was that British silver flowed to China to pay for tea. The British traders looked for something the Chinese would buy, and they found it in opium, grown in British India and smuggled into China. The East India Company grew the opium in Bengal and sold it at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who carried it to the China coast and sold it to Chinese smugglers. That way the Company could say it never sold opium in China.

According to the text, how could the East India Company say it never sold opium in China?

answers.text: It sold the opium to Chinese officials at Canton, who passed it on to the emperor.
answers.feedback: The passage says the buyers were private traders and Chinese smugglers, not officials.

answers.text: It grew the opium in China, where the emperor allowed it to be sold freely.
answers.feedback: The passage says the opium was grown in Bengal and smuggled into China, not sold with the emperor's leave.

answers.text: It sold the opium only to the British government, which shipped it to China.
answers.feedback: The passage names private traders as the buyers, not the British government.

answers.text: It sold the opium at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who carried it to China.
answers.feedback: The Company's sale ended in Calcutta, and private traders took the opium from there.

questions.text:
The Shah ruled as a modernizer. In the 1960s his "White Revolution" gave land to peasants, gave women the vote, and built schools and factories. But he ruled as an autocrat, banned real opposition, and relied on a secret police called SAVAK. Oil money flowed in, and the gap between the wealthy and the poor grew.

Which choice would best support the conclusion that many Iranians turned against the Shah?

answers.text: Iran's oil was developed by a British company.
answers.feedback: This is true, but it says nothing about how Iranians felt toward the Shah.

answers.text: In January 1978 students and clerics protested in Qom, and police killed some of them.
answers.feedback: Public protests against the government, met by killings, show opposition. This is direct evidence.

answers.text: Britain answered Mossadegh's oil law with a boycott that choked Iran's income.
answers.feedback: This is true, but it concerns Mossadegh and Britain, not Iranians' view of the Shah.

answers.text: The White Revolution gave women the vote and built schools and factories.
answers.feedback: These reforms are in the passage as the Shah's modernizing side, and they do not show opposition.

questions.text:
Metternich saw this clearly, and he set out to hold the line. In 1819 a student named Karl Sand murdered the conservative writer August von Kotzebue. Metternich used the event to push the Carlsbad Decrees through the German Confederation. They put universities under watch, banned student societies, and censored the press. Spies and police were common. Revolts that broke out in Spain and Naples in 1820 were put down by foreign troops. Austrian soldiers marched into Naples, and in 1823 a French army crossed the Pyrenees into Spain. Britain refused to take part.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Metternich won the support of all the great powers, Britain included, for crushing revolts.
answers.feedback: The last sentence says Britain refused to take part, so not every great power joined him.

answers.text: Metternich met demands for national states with censorship at home and foreign armies abroad.
answers.feedback: It joins the two parts of the passage: control at home through the Decrees, and foreign troops against revolts abroad.

answers.text: Metternich thought that student societies and a free press would strengthen the German Confederation.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says he banned student societies and censored the press.

answers.text: Metternich gave way to the revolts of 1820 after a student murdered a writer.
answers.feedback: The murder gave Metternich a reason to act, and the revolts were put down by foreign troops, so he did not give way.

discussions.title: Discussion: Is Globalization Uniting or Dividing the World?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Is Globalization Uniting or Dividing the World?
The Modern World
10 points · threaded discussion
◉ ◌ ◉
Before you start

Finish both lessons first. Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you post. Then post your answer here and reply to one classmate.

DISCUSSION PROMPT

Trade, shipping containers, the internet, and shared science have tied the world together and lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty. The lessons also show factory towns that lost their jobs, countries that gained little, fears for local customs, and attacks and diseases that crossed borders as quickly as goods. In the course's last discussion, use everything you have read since the fall of Rome.

Take a position. Is globalization uniting or dividing the world? Support your position with at least two specific details from the lessons, and include one detail that points the other way. Explain why you weigh the evidence as you do.

Aim for about 150 to 200 words.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a detail from the lessons that they did not use. If not, explain respectfully where it falls short, and point to a detail from the lessons that supports your view.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
Criteria Substantive (full credit) Thin (partial credit) Missing (no credit)
Claim and evidence
5 pts		 Takes a clear position, supports it with at least two specific details from the lessons, and deals fairly with a detail that points the other way. Takes a position but gives only one detail, or stays general, or ignores the opposing detail. No post, or no clear position.
Response to a classmate
5 pts		 Answers a specific point in a classmate's post and either strengthens it with a new detail or explains politely where it falls short. Replies in general terms, such as agreeing or disagreeing without a detail from the lessons. No reply.
10 pts total
